extracted.intended_audience: EPA policymakers, agency staff, environmental lawyers, policy analysts, and regulatory commenters
extracted.subtask_description: Public-comment legal and scientific critique of EPA's 2025 Reconsideration of the 2009 Endangerment Finding, explaining legal and evidentiary standards the Agency must meet and cataloging scientific evidence supporting continued endangerment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the Social Cost of Carbon (SCC) in cost-benefit analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigorous cost-benefit analysis requires using the SCC to estimate emissions impacts; omitting the SCC from analysis conceals large and uneven damages, particularly in health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The SCC should be included when estimating the benefits of emissions reductions. The document explains that excluding the SCC understates damages and that SCC application is standard practice (used by Government of Canada and U.S. states). It also notes SCC estimates rise as new quantified damages are incorporated and that many impacts remain unquantified so SCCs are generally lower-bound estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal 2023 SCC guidance: central 2% real discount rate and inclusion of health and labor damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal guidance from 2023 reasonably adopted a 2% central real discount rate, alongside inclusion of empirically based health and labor damages, which substantially increased values compared with legacy integrated assessment models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt empirically justified discounting (2% central real rate per 2023 guidance) and include empirically based health and labor damages when estimating SCC. The guidance recognized updated methodology increases SCC and that such updates are normal empirical calibration.

rubrics_metrics.name: SCC estimates are lower-bound and must incorporate newly quantified, peer-reviewed damages
rubrics_metrics.description: SCC estimates have risen partly due to incorporating newly quantified damages as they pass peer review and reach sufficient robustness for inclusion; since many climate impacts remain unquantified, SCC values are generally understood to be lower-bound estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As robust, peer-reviewed quantifications of impacts (e.g., health costs of wildfire smoke) become available they should be incorporated into SCC estimates. The comments cite recent studies (e.g., wildfire smoke costs ~$15/ton CO2) and emphasize the ongoing process of including additional damage categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of uncertainty — uncertainty is not a rationale for exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Uncertainty in modeling or remaining unknowns does not justify excluding damages or tools like the SCC from analysis; rigorous policy must incorporate the full range of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model updates and revised assumptions are a standard feature of modeling outcomes and do not undermine validity. Agencies must incorporate uncertainty and the full range of evidence rather than use uncertainty as a basis to omit important considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for tipping points and fat-tail/catastrophic risks (Weitzman-style reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tipping points and low-probability extreme warming outcomes imply very large damages; even a small chance of extreme warming can justify strong climate action and dramatically increase SCC estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comments cite Dietz et al. and Weitzman literature showing that accounting for tipping points and tail uncertainty can increase SCC estimates (e.g., estimates could be 6 to 200 times higher). Agencies should factor these uncertainties and tipping-point risks into economic valuation and decisionmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soundness, integrity, and transparency of IPCC and NCA reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Leading scientific assessments (IPCC, USGCRP/NCA) are undergirded by robust, high-integrity, and transparent procedures that enhance the soundness of the conclusions they reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency reliance on such assessments is appropriate because they are rigorously reviewed by the expert community and government scientists. The comments contrast these procedures with weaknesses in the Draft CWG Report and argue EPA should rely on assessments with transparent, peer-reviewed methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to acknowledge and explain departures from prior agency factual findings
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency proposes to depart from prior factual findings, it has a duty to provide a detailed explanation for the departure, a duty that is heightened when prior findings are consistent over a long period and supported by detailed evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's 2025 Reconsideration must acknowledge the decade-and-a-half record reaffirming the Endangerment Finding and explain any departure; merely stating alternative hypotheses without addressing prior findings is arbitrary and capricious. Rescinding prior denials or findings without explanation is unlawful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human activities are the primary driver of rising atmospheric greenhouse gases
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA has consistently found—and the scientific record supports—that human activities are intensifying the greenhouse effect and are the predominant cause of increased atmospheric concentrations of CO2, CH4, N2O, and fluorinated gases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should rely on extensive reviews of peer-reviewed assessments (IPCC, USGCRP, NRC) and EPA rulemaking records showing anthropogenic causality. The comments cite EPA findings across rulemakings and denials of petitions reaffirming anthropogenic attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: There has been an unprecedented rise in atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Current atmospheric GHG concentrations are elevated and essentially unprecedented levels due to historic and current anthropogenic emissions; observational records (e.g., Mauna Loa CO2) document continued increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should reference empirical concentration records (CO2 ppm, methane ppb) and trends showing recent years among the warmest on record. EPA must not ignore regulatory findings documenting these observed increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greenhouse gases cause warming and observable climate system changes
rubrics_metrics.description: The six well-mixed greenhouse gases constitute the largest anthropogenic driver of climate change; warming is unequivocal and evident in increased global air and ocean temperatures, melting snow and ice, and rising sea level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency assessments should point to observed changes (sea level rise, temperature records, shrinking ice) and documented increases in extreme events, precipitation changes, ocean acidification, and biological system changes as direct evidence of warming effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-induced climate change harms public health and welfare across many domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Climate change has the potential to affect essentially every aspect of human health, society, and the natural environment, including air quality, increases in temperatures, extreme weather events, food- and water-borne pathogens, aeroallergens, food production, water resources, infrastructure, and ecosystems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory findings and rules should explicitly consider health and welfare impacts (e.g., air quality, heat, wildfires, infectious disease risks) and cite major assessments showing advances in understanding these impacts since 2009.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on comprehensive, peer-reviewed scientific assessments and regulatory history
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's Endangerment Finding and subsequent reaffirmations appropriately relied on comprehensive assessments (IPCC, USGCRP, NAS/NRC) and a broad regulatory record; these assessments were rigorously reviewed and provide an authoritative evidentiary basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments and agency decisions should ground conclusions in the suite of major assessments and in EPA's regulatory history (standards, denials of petitions, and rulemakings). The prior denials and regulatory decisions constitute relevant precedent that EPA must consider and explain if it seeks to overturn.
